name: Khecheopalri
tagline: The wishing lake where no leaf is left on the water
meta_description: Khecheopalri Lake guide: the sacred wishing lake near Pelling, its stories, how to get there by jeep or car, homestays, costs and the best time to go.
summary: Khecheopalri is a sacred lake at about 1,700 m in West Sikkim, 25–30 km from Pelling, revered by Buddhists and Hindus alike. A short path leads through forest to a prayer-flag jetty on still green water. Most people visit on a half-day trip from Pelling; a night in a village homestay gives you the quiet hours.

local_story.title: Sho Dzo Sho: the lake that was asked to sit
paras: Long before it had a car park, this lake had a name that sounds like an invitation. Its older name, Sho Dzo Sho, is usually translated as 'O lady, sit here'. The name Khecheopalri itself is often read as Kha-Chot-Palri, 'heaven of Padmasambhava', the Indian teacher whom Sikkim's Buddhists call Guru Rinpoche. The whole surrounding country is part of Demazong, the 'hidden valley of rice' that, in Buddhist tradition, Guru Rinpoche blessed and kept hidden as a refuge for later generations.

The local story about the lake's shape is shared by two faiths. Seen from the ridge above, the outline of the water is said to resemble a footprint. Buddhist pilgrims say it is the footprint of Tara, the female Buddha of compassion; Hindu pilgrims say it is the footprint of Shiva. Both come here to light butter lamps or incense, tie prayer flags and make a wish, which is why it is often called the wishing lake.

The best-known piece of lore is about the trees. Forest grows close around the water, yet people here will tell you that the surface stays clear because birds pick up any leaf that falls on it. Whatever you make of that, the lake is cared for: boating, fishing and swimming are not allowed, shoes come off on the jetty, and visitors are asked to keep their voices low. In the early morning, before the day trippers from Pelling arrive, it is the quietest place on the West Sikkim circuit.

did_you_know: The lake's older name, Sho Dzo Sho, is usually translated as 'O lady, sit here'; Khecheopalri is often read as Kha-Chot-Palri, 'heaven of Padmasambhava'.
Seen from the ridge above, the lake's outline is said to resemble a footprint: of Tara for Buddhist pilgrims, of Shiva for Hindu pilgrims.
Boating, fishing and swimming are not allowed, and local belief holds that forest birds remove any leaf that falls on the water.
intro: The lake lies in a forested bowl below Khecheopalri village, about 25–30 km from Pelling by a road that branches off the route to Yuksom. Cars stop at a small parking area with tea stalls and shops selling incense and prayer flags. From there a paved path of a few hundred metres leads through the trees to a wooden jetty draped with flags, where you look across the water to the forest on the far side. The walk is flat and short enough for seniors and small children.

Most visitors give it an hour on a Pelling sightseeing loop, together with Rimbi Falls and Kanchenjunga Falls. That is fine, but the lake is at its best early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the cars have gone and the birds are active. If you can, spend a night in one of the simple homestays nearby and walk up to the village and its small gompa. Indians need no permit; foreign nationals need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit.
facts: Patchy; often weak at the lake itself
costs: Pelling sightseeing car with Khecheopalri and the falls
Village homestay with dinner and breakfast
Butter lamps, incense or a prayer flag

highlights.title: The prayer-flag jetty
highlights.text: A wooden walkway runs out over the water under rows of prayer flags. Take off your shoes, walk slowly and stand at the end to look across the lake to the forest. Early morning light, with mist lifting off the water, is the time photographers wait for.

highlights.title: A lake shared by two faiths
highlights.text: Buddhist and Hindu pilgrims both come here, seeing in the outline of the lake the footprint of Tara or of Shiva. You will see butter lamps, incense and prayer wheels side by side. Watch quietly, and if you want to make a wish, light a lamp at the stand.

highlights.title: Khecheopalri village and gompa
highlights.text: Above the lake, the farming village of Khecheopalri has its own small gompa and wide views over the valley. A steady uphill walk or a short drive takes you there. It is where most homestays are, and where you see everyday life beyond the tea stalls.

highlights.title: Birds in the lake forest
highlights.text: The broadleaf forest around the water is good for birdwatching in the quiet hours. Sunbirds, laughingthrushes, minivets and barbets are among the birds people commonly see in forests like this. Bring binoculars and walk the path slowly before 8 am; sightings are never guaranteed.

highlights.title: Waterfalls on the way
highlights.text: The road from Pelling passes Rimbi Falls and Kanchenjunga Falls, both standard stops on a sightseeing loop. They run hardest in September and October after the monsoon. Combine them with the lake for a half-day trip that costs ₹2,500–3,500 for the whole car.

how_to_reach.text: The simplest way: a Pelling sightseeing car covering Khecheopalri, Rimbi Falls and Kanchenjunga Falls costs about ₹2,500–3,500 for the vehicle, 25–30 km each way and about an hour of driving. Shared by four or five people, it is cheap. Fares are indicative.

A small number of shared jeeps run between Geyzing and Khecheopalri, usually leaving Geyzing in the afternoon and returning the next morning, roughly ₹100–150 a seat. That timing suits travellers staying overnight. Check current timings at the Geyzing stand or with your hotel.

An old footpath links Khecheopalri with Yuksom over the forested ridge, and some trekkers walk it as part of a monastery trail. It takes most of a day. Go only with a local guide (₹1,500–2,500 a day), ask about trail conditions, and avoid it in the monsoon.

where_to_stay: There are no hotels at the lake, only a handful of simple homestays and lodges near the parking area and in Khecheopalri village on the ridge above. Expect ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast, home-cooked food, shared bathrooms in some places and very cold nights from December to February. Electricity and hot water can be irregular, so carry a torch and warm layers. If you prefer more comfort, stay in Pelling, 25–30 km away, and visit on a half-day trip, coming early in the morning to beat the crowds.
tips: Reach the lake before 9 am or after 3 pm to avoid the busiest hours of the Pelling sightseeing cars.
Take off your shoes on the jetty, walk clockwise around prayer wheels and do not throw coins, food or flowers into the water.
Carry a light rain jacket even in clear months, because cloud often settles in the lake bowl by midday.
If you stay overnight, bring a torch and warm clothes; homestay power and hot water can be irregular.
Combine the lake with Rimbi Falls and Kanchenjunga Falls in one car to split the ₹2,500–3,500 fare among more people.

experiences.title: First hour on the prayer-flag jetty
experiences.cost: Small entry or parking fee · lamps ₹20–100
experiences.summary: Walk the forest path to the jetty at Khecheopalri soon after sunrise, when mist lifts off the water and only villagers are about. Light a butter lamp, make a wish if you like, and sit long enough to watch for a leaf on the water.
body: This works best if you sleep near the lake or leave Pelling at about 6 am by car. From the parking area the paved path runs for a few hundred metres through tall trees, past prayer wheels and a few shrines. In the first hour after sunrise you mostly share it with villagers turning the wheels on their way to work, and the sound of the forest is louder than any voice. Keep to one side so people can pass.

At the jetty, take off your shoes and walk slowly to the end under rows of prayer flags. Mist often hangs over the water until the sun clears the ridge, then burns off in minutes, and the forest reflects in the still surface. Buddhist pilgrims light butter lamps and recite prayers here; Hindu pilgrims come for the footprint of Shiva they see in the lake's outline. You are welcome to light a lamp at the stand for a small offering.

Then sit and watch. The local story is that birds pick up any leaf that falls on the water, and many visitors spend a quiet while looking for one. Keep your voice low, do not feed fish or birds, and do not throw coins or flowers. By 9 or 10 am the first sightseeing cars arrive from Pelling and the jetty fills with groups, so this is the hour to have the lake almost to yourself.

faqs.q: What time does Khecheopalri Lake open?
faqs.a: The lake is a place of worship as well as a tourist stop, and villagers use the path from early morning. Ticketed or parking entry for visitors usually runs in daylight hours, roughly from early morning to late afternoon. Arrive around 6.30–8 am for the quietest time, and check current timings and fees locally.

faqs.q: Can we boat or swim in Khecheopalri Lake?
faqs.a: No. The lake is sacred to Buddhists and Hindus, and boating, fishing and swimming are not allowed. Visitors are also asked not to throw coins, flowers or food into the water. You can walk the path, stand on the jetty, light lamps and photograph the lake, keeping your voice low.

faqs.q: Is the lake path suitable for elderly visitors?
faqs.a: Yes. The path from the parking area to the jetty is a few hundred metres, paved and nearly level, with a few steps. Most seniors manage it at an easy pace. It can be slippery after rain, so wear shoes with grip. Shoes come off on the jetty, so wear socks in cold months.

experiences.title: Up to Khecheopalri village and its gompa
experiences.summary: Leave the lake behind and walk up to Khecheopalri village on the ridge, with its small gompa, terraced fields and views over the valley. It shows you the farming life that sustains the lake's caretakers, and it is where most homestays are.
body: Most visitors see only the lake and the tea stalls. Above them, on the ridge, is Khecheopalri village, where the families who look after the lake live and farm. Ask at the parking area for the footpath up; it climbs steadily through forest and fields, and takes most people 45 minutes to an hour. You can also drive up by the road, but walking gives you the changing views back over the lake bowl and across the valley.

The village gompa is small and simple, a working prayer hall for the local Buddhist community rather than a showpiece. It may be locked outside prayer times; if someone is there, ask before you enter, take off your shoes and walk clockwise. Around it are prayer flags, chortens and the terraced fields of maize, millet and vegetables, with large cardamom in the shaded, damper patches. From the ridge, on a clear day, you can see far across West Sikkim.

This walk is best combined with a homestay night, so you are not rushing back to a car. Late afternoon is good for the light and for seeing farm work wind down; morning is better for birds and clear views. Carry water and a rain jacket, wear shoes with grip, and ask before photographing people or homes. If you are walking down to the lake afterwards, do it before dusk, as the forest path is unlit.

faqs.q: How far is Khecheopalri village from the lake?
faqs.a: The village sits on the ridge above the lake. On foot it takes about 45 minutes to an hour uphill on a forest and field path, and less coming down. A road also reaches the village, so you can drive up and walk down. Ask locally for the path, as it is not well signposted.

faqs.q: Is Khecheopalri gompa open to visitors?
faqs.a: It is a small village monastery used by the local community, not a staffed tourist site. The hall may be locked outside prayer times. If a monk or caretaker is present, ask politely before entering, take off your shoes and follow their guidance on photographs. A small donation is welcome.

faqs.q: Are there homestays in Khecheopalri village?
faqs.a: Yes, a few simple family homestays operate in the village and near the lake, charging about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast. Facilities are basic and nights are cold in winter. Book through a Pelling hotel or agent, or ask at the lake parking area on arrival outside the busy weeks of October and May.

experiences.title: Birding walk in the lake forest
experiences.summary: The broadleaf forest around Khecheopalri is quiet, sheltered and good for birds in the early morning. Walk the lake path and the village lanes slowly with binoculars, listen more than you look, and leave before the day trippers arrive.
body: Khecheopalri sits in a bowl of mixed broadleaf forest at about 1,700 m, the kind of habitat that holds many of Sikkim's mid-altitude birds. Because the lake is sacred and the forest around it is protected by custom as well as rules, it is quieter than most roadside spots. The first two hours after sunrise are when birds are most active and the path is empty, which is exactly when most visitors are still in Pelling.

Walk slowly along the path to the jetty and back, then up the lanes towards the village. Listen for flocks moving through the canopy. Birds commonly seen in forests like this include sunbirds, laughingthrushes, minivets, barbets, bulbuls, tits and warblers, and in winter more species come down from higher up the hills. Sightings are never guaranteed. A pair of 8x or 10x binoculars and a field guide or app for the Indian subcontinent will make the walk much richer.

If you are serious about birds, ask your homestay whether someone in the village knows them well; local knowledge counts for more than any list. Keep to the paths, do not use playback calls near the sacred lake, and keep noise low. Wear dull colours and carry a light rain jacket. From June to September leeches are common in the forest, so we suggest skipping the walk in those months or wearing leech socks.

faqs.q: What birds can we see at Khecheopalri?
faqs.a: The forest around the lake holds typical mid-altitude Sikkim birds. Sunbirds, laughingthrushes, minivets, barbets, bulbuls, tits and warblers are among those commonly seen in similar forests, with more species in winter. Exact sightings vary with season and luck, so treat any list as a guide, not a promise.

faqs.q: When is the best time for birdwatching here?
faqs.a: Early morning from October to May, roughly 6–8.30 am, before the sightseeing cars arrive from Pelling. Winter brings altitudinal migrants down from higher forests, and spring brings breeding calls. The monsoon months are wet, misty and full of leeches, so most birders avoid June to September.

faqs.q: Do we need a guide for birding at Khecheopalri?
faqs.a: Not for the lake path, which is short and easy to follow. A local who knows the birds will help you find and name far more species, and a day's guide costs roughly ₹1,500–2,500. Ask your homestay or a Pelling agent. Whatever you do, keep to paths and avoid playback near the sacred lake.

experiences.title: A homestay supper of gundruk and churpi
experiences.cost: Included in homestay ₹1,500–2,500 pp with breakfast
experiences.summary: Spend a night in a Khecheopalri homestay and eat what the family eats: rice, dal, local greens, gundruk, perhaps churpi and a fiery dalle chilli pickle, cooked on a wood or gas fire. It is the cheapest and warmest way to understand the village.
body: Homestay dinners in West Sikkim are simple and filling. Expect rice, a lentil dal, a vegetable or two from the garden, and often a dish of local greens such as nettle (sisnu) or ferns (ningro) in season. Many families keep gundruk, fermented and dried leafy greens, for soups and pickles, especially in winter. You may also be offered churpi, a local cheese made from cow or yak milk, either soft and cooked into a curry or hard for chewing.

The kitchen is usually the warmest room in the house, and guests are often welcome to sit near the fire while the meal is cooked. Ask before you take photographs, offer to help, and do not be shy about asking what something is. Most homes have a jar of pickle made with dalle khursani, the small round chilli of Sikkim and Darjeeling, which is hotter than it looks. Try a tiny piece first. Breakfast might be sel roti, puri or bread with tea.

Some homes brew chhang or tongba, millet beer drunk through a bamboo straw from a wooden or bamboo mug, especially in the cold months. Drink it only if you wish; no one will mind if you say no. Dinner is early, often by 7 or 7.30 pm, and the village goes quiet soon after, so bring a book and warm layers. Settle the bill in cash, as cards and UPI may not work.

faqs.q: What food is served in Khecheopalri homestays?
faqs.a: Usually home-style meals: rice, dal, seasonal vegetables and local greens, with pickles. Depending on the season and family, you may get gundruk, churpi, nettle soup or ferns, and sel roti or puri at breakfast. Tell your hosts early about allergies or if you are vegetarian or vegan; most homes cook vegetarian food easily.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drink tongba or chhang?
faqs.a: Tongba and chhang are traditional millet drinks made at home in many hill villages and are usually mild. Drink in moderation, especially at altitude, and skip them if you are taking medicines, pregnant, driving or simply prefer not to. Hosts will not be offended if you politely decline and ask for tea instead.

faqs.q: How do we pay at a village homestay?
faqs.a: Carry cash. Mobile signal is patchy around the lake, so UPI and cards may not work when you need them. Rates of ₹1,500–2,500 per person usually include dinner and breakfast; extra tea, snacks or packed lunches may cost a little more. Confirm the rate and what it includes before you settle in.

faqs.q: How far is Khecheopalri Lake from Pelling?
faqs.a: About 25–30 km, roughly an hour each way by car on a road that branches off the route to Yuksom. Most people visit on a half-day loop that includes Rimbi Falls and Kanchenjunga Falls, costing ₹2,500–3,500 for a reserved car. A few shared jeeps run from Geyzing, mostly in the afternoon.

faqs.q: Is Khecheopalri Lake worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you come at the right time. In the early morning or late afternoon it is one of the quietest and most beautiful spots in West Sikkim, with a prayer-flag jetty over still water and forest all round. At midday in October it can be crowded with groups, so time your visit to avoid the rush.

faqs.q: Why is it called the wishing lake?
faqs.a: Buddhist and Hindu pilgrims both believe that prayers and wishes made here are heard. Buddhists link the lake to Guru Rinpoche and Tara, and Hindus see Shiva's footprint in its outline. Pilgrims light butter lamps, tie prayer flags and make a wish at the jetty. Visitors are welcome to do the same, quietly.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Khecheopalri Lake?
faqs.a: A small entry or parking fee has usually been charged, in the range of ₹10–50, and you may spend a little more on butter lamps or prayer flags. Fees change, so check current rates at the gate. There is no charge for walking the path to the jetty once you are in.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Khecheopalri?
faqs.a: October to December and March to May are best, with dry paths and clearer skies. Winter mornings are cold and often misty over the water, which many photographers love. June to September brings heavy rain, leeches and landslides on the road. At any time of year, come early in the day.

faqs.q: Can we stay overnight at Khecheopalri?
faqs.a: Yes, in a handful of simple homestays and lodges near the lake and in the village above, at about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast. Facilities are basic and winter nights are cold. An overnight stay lets you see the lake at dawn before the day trippers, which is the main reason to do it.

faqs.q: Do foreigners need a permit for Khecheopalri?
faqs.a: Foreign nationals need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, which covers Pelling, Yuksom and the lake. It is issued online or at entry points such as Rangpo and Melli. Indians do not need any permit. Carry passport and visa copies, and check current status before you travel, as rules change.

faqs.q: What should we wear and do at the lake?
faqs.a: Dress modestly, carry a warm layer and a rain jacket, and wear easy-to-remove shoes because they come off on the jetty. Walk clockwise around prayer wheels, keep your voice low, and do not throw coins, flowers or food into the water. Ask before photographing pilgrims at prayer.

faqs.q: Can we combine Khecheopalri with Yuksom in one day?
faqs.a: Yes. Khecheopalri lies off the Pelling–Yuksom road, so a reserved car can do Pelling, the falls, the lake and Yuksom in one long day for about ₹3,000–4,000. Better still, visit the lake on your way to a night in Yuksom, so you are not racing back to Pelling before dark.
